title: Retrospective study to evaluate the risk of recurrence of aneurysmal bone cysts
summary:
Bone cysts are among the most common tumour-like lesions of the bone. A distinction is made between the ‘simple’ juvenile bone cyst, a lesion filled with serous fluid, which is diagnosed in almost 80% of cases in the first and second decade of life and only becomes symptomatic in fractures and is usually an incidental finding, and the aneurysmal bone cyst. As we know today, this is a neoplasia with chromosomal translocation (t(16;17)(q22;p13)).[5] Aneurysmal bone cysts (ACC) are basically present in two forms: the primary form, which actually corresponds to a primary lesion - only this shows the translocation - and the secondary form, which is a reactive concomitant lesion in another neoplastic or non-neoplastic process of the bone. The distinction is essential, as the primary lesion of a secondary ACZ could well be malignant or would require a different therapy. In the differential diagnosis, a telangiectatic osteosarcoma must be excluded. Histologically, the ACZ appears to be filled with various blood-filled cavities, subdivided by connective tissue septa, which contain small balls of osteoid and osteoclast giant cells. With an incidence of around 3-4% of all registered bone tumours, it is rare and is mainly found in the 2nd decade of life.[4] The symptoms are non-specific and treatment consists of curettage, possibly with adjuvants and filling of the lesion. Marginal resections are rarely possible. Radiographically, the lesion appears metaphyseal, in the early stages as eccentric osteolysis, in the later stages with distension of the bone and shell-like neocortical bone.[1] Prognostically, children under the age of 10 are particularly prone to local recurrence. The intralesional application of inflammation-inducing reagents or vascular embolisation is possible and is discussed in different ways. The latter can significantly optimise the intraoperative overview and blood loss, especially before curettage in difficult locations (e.g. pelvis)[6]. In exceptional cases, low-dose radiotherapy can be discussed[2]. In recent years, an IgG2 anti-RANKL antibody (denosumab) has also been introduced into therapy for critical locations[3].
The aim of this study is to retrospectively evaluate the clinical and radiological appearance of the lesion as well as the therapy carried out and its success in the approximately 70 patients treated in our clinic to date.

interventions.name: All patients with ACZ of the bone with surgical intervention at the study clinic. Clinical courses and the results of technical examinations (imaging) are recorded at the time of their collection in routine diagnostics.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
All patients with ACZ of the bone with surgical intervention at the study clinic during the study period.
Exclusion criteria:
None
